cues.text: I haven't seen you for a bit, Marie.
cues.speaker: Colin

cues.text: No, I've been busy with my project.
cues.speaker: Marie

cues.text: You're making a vegan alternative to eggs, aren't you? Something that doesn't use animal products.
cues.speaker: Colin

cues.text: Yes, I'm using chickpeas. I had two main aims when I first started looking for an alternative to eggs, but actually I've found chickpeas have got more advantages.
cues.speaker: Marie

cues.text: Right.
cues.speaker: Colin

cues.text: But how about your project on reusing waste food? You were looking at bread, weren't you?
cues.speaker: Marie

cues.text: Yes, it's been hard work, but I've enjoyed it. The basic process was quite straightforward, breaking the stale bread down to a paste, then reforming it.
cues.speaker: Colin

cues.text: But you were using 3D printing, weren't you, to make the paste into biscuits?
cues.speaker: Marie

cues.text: Yeah, I'd used that before, but in this project, I had time to play around with different patterns for the biscuits and finding how I could add fruit and vegetables to make them a more appetising colour, and I was pleased with what I managed to produce.
cues.speaker: Colin

cues.text: It must have been a great feeling to make something appetising out of bits of old bread that would have been thrown away otherwise.
cues.speaker: Marie

cues.text: It was. And I'm hoping that some of the restaurants in town will be interested in the biscuits. I'm going to send them some samples.
cues.speaker: Colin

cues.text: I came across something on the internet yesterday that might interest you. It was a company that's developed touch-sensitive sensors for food labels. It's a special sort of label on the food package. When the label's smooth, the food is fresh. And then when you can feel bumps on the label, that means the food's gone bad. It started off as a project to help visually impaired people know whether food was fit to eat or not.
cues.speaker: Marie

cues.text: Interesting. So just solid food?
cues.speaker: Colin

cues.text: No. Things like milk and juice as well. But actually I thought it might be really good for drug storage in hospitals and pharmacies.
cues.speaker: Marie

cues.text: Right. And coming back to food, maybe it would be possible to use it for other things besides freshness, like how many kilograms a joint of meat is, for example.
cues.speaker: Colin

cues.text: Yes, there's all sorts of possibilities.
cues.speaker: Marie

cues.text: I was reading an article about food trends predicting how eating habits might change in the next few years.
cues.speaker: Colin

cues.text: Oh, things like more focus on local products. That seems so obvious, but the shops are still full of imported foods.
cues.speaker: Marie

cues.text: Yes, they need to be more proactive to address that.
cues.speaker: Colin

cues.text: And somehow motivate consumers to change, yes.
cues.speaker: Marie

cues.text: One thing everyone's aware of is the need for a reduction in unnecessary packaging. But just about everything you buy in supermarkets is still covered in plastic. The government needs to do something about it.
cues.speaker: Colin

cues.text: Absolutely, it's got to change.
cues.speaker: Marie

cues.text: Do you think there'll be more interest in gluten and lactose-free food?
cues.speaker: Colin

cues.text: For people with allergies or food intolerances, I don't know. Lots of people I know have been buying that type of food for years now.
cues.speaker: Marie

cues.text: Yes, even if they haven't been diagnosed with an allergy.
cues.speaker: Colin

cues.text: That's right. One thing I've noticed is the number of branded products related to celebrity chefs. People watch them cooking on TV and then buy things like spice mixes or frozen foods with the chef's name on. I bought something like that once, but I won't again.
cues.speaker: Marie

cues.text: Yeah, I bought a ready -made spice mix for chicken which was supposed to be used by a chef I'd seen on television. And it didn't actually taste of anything.
cues.speaker: Colin

cues.text: Hmm, did the article mention ghost kitchens used to produce takeaway food?
cues.speaker: Marie

cues.text: No, what are they?
cues.speaker: Colin

cues.text: Well, they might have the name of a restaurant, but actually they're a cooking facility just for delivery meals. The public don't ever go there. But people aren't aware of that. It's all kept very quiet.
cues.speaker: Marie

cues.text: So people don't realise the food's not actually from the restaurant?
cues.speaker: Colin

cues.text: Right.
cues.speaker: Marie

cues.text: Did you know more and more people are using all sorts of different mushrooms now to treat different health concerns? Things like heart problems.
cues.speaker: Colin

cues.text: Hmm, they might be taking a big risk there.
cues.speaker: Marie

cues.text: Yes, it's hard to know which varieties are safe to eat. Anyway, maybe now we should...
cues.speaker: Colin
